pm_exper_user_2482_maasv_v0446_pmv2_r1.question: How can I deal with the stress of feeling like I have to constantly prove myself at work?
pm_exper_user_2482_maasv_v0446_pmv2_r1.all_options:
(a) You might find it helpful to reframe your daily wins—not just as meeting professional goals, but as making your family proud and creating a stable future for them. Setting clear boundaries between work and family time can help you stay grounded amidst competitive pressures. Conversations with trusted relatives or community members could give you perspective when your role feels overwhelming.
(b) You might find it helpful to reframe your daily wins—not just as meeting sales quotas, but as progress in building long-term trust with healthcare providers and ensuring strict FDA compliance, which is a real strength of yours. Setting clear boundaries around work time can help maintain balance, especially when the industry feels like a race. Having a mentor within the pharmaceutical network to discuss your long-term career path could make the pressure feel more purposeful.
(c) You might find it helpful to reframe your daily wins—not just as meeting job targets, but as meaningful progress in your personal and professional growth. Setting clear boundaries between work and personal life can help keep stress in check. Talking with a mentor or trusted colleague can provide perspective when the pressure feels constant.
(d) You might find it helpful to reframe your daily wins—not just in terms of hitting fitness milestones or trying new healthy recipes, but as part of building a lifestyle that sustains you outside of work. Setting clear boundaries around your workout routine can help you feel more grounded when stress builds. Having a supportive running group or cycling club could make the competitive nature of your personal goals more enjoyable.

[] It sounds like you’re carrying a sustained load of mental and emotional strain, which makes it hard to feel energized even outside work hours. Burnout often builds quietly until it becomes overwhelming, so it’s good you’re noticing it now.

One approach is to plan small, low-cost resets without feeling they have to be grand or long. A quick weekend change of scenery could be a great release, even if it’s just a simple getaway. If you do decide on a short trip, try reframing it as part of your performance strategy — investing in your rest so you can bring more focus and energy back to your work.

At the same time, see if you can delegate one or two tasks before you leave, or adjust deadlines if possible. Even symbolic breathing space in the workweek — blocking 30 minutes as a non-negotiable break — can help.

Do you want me to share a few ways to negotiate breathing room with your manager without making it a big deal?
[] You can frame the conversation in a way that emphasizes productivity and effectiveness, rather than personal struggle. For example, you might say, "I want to make sure I deliver my best work on these projects, and I’ve noticed that having a block of uninterrupted focus time really improves my output. Could we look at my schedule to create some windows for that?" This presents your request as a strategic choice that benefits the team and the quality of your work.

You can also link breathing space to project outcomes — for instance, describing how stepping away briefly allows you to return with sharper focus and fewer mistakes. Managers are more likely to respond well when they see the direct connection between your well-being and results.
